title: The Patience of Bread
focus: Gerund and infinitive (stop, remember, regret, try)

lines.text: Welcome to Kitchen Table. I'm Hana, and today Luis is here to talk about bread.
Thanks, Hana. I should confess that I tried making sourdough for years before I got it right.
What went wrong at first?
I kept baking the dough too early. I hadn't let it rise long enough, so my loaves came out flat.
And what changed?
A neighbour told me to stop checking the dough every ten minutes. Honestly, I couldn't believe how much difference it made.
So patience is the main ingredient?
Patience and a warm kitchen. In winter I remember putting the bowl next to the radiator, which helped a lot.
Some people say a starter is hard to keep alive. Is that fair?
Not really. You feed it flour and water every day, and it looks after itself. I regret not starting sooner.
Do you recommend buying special equipment?
Not at first. Try using a normal pot with a lid instead of an expensive baking stone.
That's reassuring. Any final tip for beginners?
Keep a diary. Writing down what you did helps you to repeat your successes.

title: Gardeners of the Reef

lines.text: Dr Okafor, you run a coral nursery. Can you explain what that means?
Certainly. Working in shallow water, we grow small pieces of coral on frames, then move them to damaged reefs.
Why is that necessary?
Weakened by warm seas, many reefs have stopped growing. Left alone, some would take decades to recover.
How fast do your corals grow?
Fed by clean, moving water, they can double in size within a year. That surprised even us.
Does the work ever feel hopeless?
Sometimes, yes. Having seen entire reefs turn white, I'm realistic about the risks. But I refuse to give up.
What can ordinary people do?
Choosing sunscreen that is safe for the sea is a start. Having said that, the biggest change has to come from reducing emissions.
So nursery work isn't enough on its own?
No. It buys time, but it can't replace action on climate. Anyone claiming otherwise is oversimplifying.

title: Bees Above the Traffic

lines.text: This morning we're on top of a hotel in the city centre, where four hives have been installed.
Hello, I'm Samir, the beekeeper, who looks after these hives twice a week.
Samir, most people imagine bees in the countryside. Why put them here?
City bees, which find plenty of flowers in parks and balconies, often do better than country bees.
Really? What about pollution?
It's less of a problem than you'd think. Farms, where crops are sprayed, can actually be more dangerous.
And what do you do with the honey?
The hotel kitchen, whose chef is a big fan, uses it in desserts and sauces.
Do guests ever get nervous?
A few did at first. Now we run a short talk on Saturdays, which most guests enjoy.
Isn't it risky, though?
Not if you stay calm. Bees only sting when they feel threatened, which is rare.
Will you add more hives?
We'd like to. The manager, who has been very supportive, has agreed to two more next spring.

title: Four Days Are Enough?

lines.text: Welcome to Open Floor. Tonight's question is whether companies should adopt a four day working week.
Although it sounds risky, I believe it works. Despite working fewer hours, people are often more focused.
I see the appeal, but not every job can be squeezed into four days. Hospitals and shops need staff all week.
That's true. However, even in those jobs, staff could rotate so that everyone has a long weekend.
Even if that worked, it would be expensive. Employers would have to hire more people.
Not necessarily. Some firms found that sick days fell, so they saved money in the end.
Perhaps, although those were mostly small offices. I'm not convinced the results would be the same in a factory.
Omar, what would you say to a manager who is still sceptical?
Try it for three months first. If it doesn't work, go back to the old system. Nothing is lost.
I'd agree with a trial, provided the customers don't suffer.
Julia, is that a compromise you could accept?
Yes, as long as the trial is properly measured. Otherwise we're only guessing.
Then we'll leave it there. Thank you both.

title: Why We Forget
focus: Advice and obligation (should, have to, had better)

lines.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about why we forget what we learn, and what can be done about it.
More than a century ago, a German psychologist called Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory using lists of nonsense words.
He discovered that forgetting is fastest just after learning. Within a day, a large part of the list had disappeared.
You might think the answer is to read your notes again and again, but research suggests that this is not very effective.
It feels productive, because the words look familiar. Familiar, however, is not the same as remembered.
A far better method is to test yourself. Close the book and try to write down what you can recall.
Another useful habit is spacing. Instead of studying for five hours on one night, you should study for one hour on five different days.
Each time you return to the material, your brain has to work a little harder, and that effort strengthens the memory.
Sleep also matters. Students who revise late at night and then skip sleep are not helping themselves.
I'm not saying that cramming never works. It can get you through a test tomorrow. But it's a poor way to keep knowledge for life.
So, to sum up. Test yourself, space your sessions, and sleep properly.
Next week, we'll look at how stress affects concentration. Please read the short article on the course page before then.

title: To Go or Not to Go

lines.text: Ben, you took a year off before university. Do you think I should do the same?
It depends. If I hadn't travelled, I wouldn't have learned how to manage money.
But didn't you lose time? Your friends finished before you.
A little, yes. But if I'd gone straight to university, I'd probably have dropped out.
Really? Why?
I was exhausted after school. I wouldn't have enjoyed the course if I hadn't taken a break.
My parents are worried. They'd rather I started in September.
I understand. Mine said the same, until I showed them my plan for the year.
What was in the plan?
Six months working in a cafe, then three months volunteering at a school in Peru, and the rest travelling.
Peru sounds amazing. Did you ever regret going?
Never. Though if I had saved more beforehand, I wouldn't have run out of money in the last month.
So the lesson is to have a plan and a budget.
Exactly. Don't just wander around hoping something will happen.

title: Do Language Apps Work?
focus: Reporting verbs (admit, claim, suggest, recommend, insist, deny)

lines.text: Welcome back to Mind and Method. I'm Ayesha, and this week we ask whether language apps really work.
I'm Tomas. I'll admit that I downloaded three apps last year and deleted two of them within a month.
Why did you delete them?
They claimed I'd be fluent in three months, which was nonsense. I was only memorising lists of words.
To be fair, a teacher I interviewed suggested using apps for vocabulary rather than for speaking.
That makes sense. She also recommended finding a conversation partner, even if it's only once a week.
Did she deny that apps are useful?
Not at all. She insisted that a daily habit beats a long session at the weekend, and apps make that easy.
So what's the best approach?
Combine them. Use the app for ten minutes each morning, then speak with a real person on Saturday.
I'd add that listeners should avoid apps which promise miracles.
Absolutely. If something sounds too good to be true, it usually is.
Next week we'll hear from a man who learned Korean by watching television.
I can't wait. I'm told he now works as a translator.

title: An Orchestra for Everyone

lines.text: We're in a school hall where an unusual orchestra is rehearsing. Everyone here is welcome, whatever their age.
That's the idea. The orchestra was founded six years ago by a group of parents.
And how are the instruments obtained?
Many were donated by local families, and the rest are borrowed from the town council.
Do members have to audition?
No. Nobody is ever turned away. Beginners are placed at the back, and they're helped by more experienced players.
That must be challenging for the music.
It can be. Some concerts have been spoiled by a missed note, but the audience has always been very kind.
Where is the orchestra heard outside the hall?
We've been invited to play at the hospital every December, and a concert in the park is being planned for the summer.
What has been the biggest achievement?
For me, it's seeing a shy teenager who had never touched a violin become the leader of the second violins.
That's wonderful. Is more funding needed?
Always. A new piano is badly needed, so a charity night will be held next month.
